title: Dynamic shape / sequence length handling: padding, bucketing & kernel selection (draft)
content:
Summary:

This doc captures design options and a proposed approach for handling dynamic input shapes and sequence length variability in the serving runtime. Focus areas: padding policies, bucketization strategies, mapping buckets -> kernel variants, and interactions with KV cache and scheduler. Goal is to reduce per-token cost while meeting latency SLOs and preserving model quality.

Background / motivation:
- Customer workloads show heavy tail in sequence length: many short requests (<=64 tokens), a non-negligible mid-range (65-512), and occasional long sequences (>=1024).
- Naive pad-to-max wastes compute for batches mixing short + long sequences.
- Kernel performance is highly shape-dependent: certain attention kernels (flash/fused) and quantized kernels perform very well at specific sequence dims and head sizes.
- KV cache reuse and prefix caching can reduce cost, but cache hit interactions with bucketization must be correct (cache keys must reflect effective padded length or bucket id as needed).

Design goals / constraints:
- Keep tail latency within configured SLOs (p95/p99 targets per tier).
- Optimize for cost (tokens/sec per GPU), especially for hosted API where unit economics matter.
- Minimize user-visible regressions in served outputs (no change to model semantics).
- Implement incrementally with safe fallbacks.

High level approach (proposal):
1) Lightweight online profiling to build per-model seq-length distribution (histogram + quantiles).
2) Derive a small set of buckets from the distribution (6-8 buckets typical): e.g. [<=32], (33-64], (65-128], (129-256], (257-512], (513-1024], (>1024). Bucket boundaries are tunable per model/profile.
3) For each bucket: select a padding policy and kernel variant.\n   - padding policy: pad-to-bucket-max (tight), pad-to-power-of-two (optional for kernels that prefer pow2), or no-pad with intra-batch dynamic kernels.
   - kernel variant: e.g., flash-attn-2, fused-attn-quant, generic-cuda, int8-quant-kernel-x.
4) Scheduling: group requests by bucket at the front of scheduling queue (a short coalescing window, e.g., 2-6ms) to form continuous batches with similar shapes.
5) KV cache: cache entries keyed by (model-id, session-id, effective-sequence-length, bucket-id, kv-format-version) so that reuse is safe when bucket/shape mapping changes.

Padding policies (tradeoffs):
- No padding (native variable-shape kernels): lowest work but requires kernels and batching infrastructure to accept ragged inputs. Complexity: higher implementation cost, scheduling fragmentation increases, potential loss of vectorization.
- Pad-to-max-in-batch: simplest, but if a long request is in the batch it penalizes all peers. Works okay when we pre-bucket.
- Pad-to-bucket-max (recommended): pad only up to the bucket's max length (tight). Limits wasted tokens while enabling efficient kernel dispatch.
- Pad-to-aligned-chunk (e.g., pow2 or multiple of 8): beneficial for kernels that have alignment requirements for memory coalescing. Use only for buckets where kernel benchmarks show wins.

Bucketing strategies (detailed):
- Static boundaries: simple, set from offline analysis for common models. Low overhead.
- Quantile-based boundaries: compute boundaries that equalize request counts per bucket. Good for balancing scheduler load.
- Cost-aware buckets (recommended): choose boundaries to trade latency vs. cost using an objective function (minimize expected token-work subject to latency constraints). Use offline profiling + online feedback.
- Adaptive online re-bucketing: update boundaries slowly (daily/weekly) based on traffic drift. Must be versioned and rolling-updated to avoid cache/key incompatibility or sudden scheduler churn.

Kernel selection mapping:
- Maintain a per-model kernel profile table: for each bucket -> ranked list of kernel candidates with measured throughput/latency/peak-memory on each target hw type.
- Kernel profiler runs offline using representative batches for each bucket. Capture: tokens/sec, p50/p95 latency, memory headroom. Store profiler results in redis/metadata store.
- Runtime mapping: choose first kernel that meets latency SLO and maximizes throughput (or lowest cost per token). If none meet SLO, select fallback lowest-latency kernel.

Scheduling integration and batching windows:
- Use a short coalescing window (adaptive based on qps and observed latency) to form batches by bucket.
- Enqueue requests into per-bucket queues; a small global allocator fills worker batches from bucket queues respecting priority & SLOs.
- For low-qps buckets we may allow cross-bucket coalescing with pad-to-bucket-max approach if it improves utilization. This should be gated by experiment flags.

KV cache interactions and correctness notes:
- Cache key must incorporate the effective (unpadded) sequence length or a canonical representation so a cached KV chunk can be reused regardless of padding. We prefer keying by raw sequence length and bucket id to make invalidation explicit.
- When we change bucket boundaries, we must bump kv-format-version and/or invalidate affected cache entries to avoid mismatches between cached positional encodings/offsets.
- Cache sharding: store KV per-session with metadata about the bucket version used to produce it. On bucket-change, either recompute or retrofit by trimming/padding cache during replay.

Metrics & experimental plan:
- Offline: run profiler across models/hw combos to produce kernel tables. Compare pad-to-bucket vs no-pad vs pad-to-max. Collect tokens/sec and p95 latency.
- Online A/B: rollout bucketed padding to a subset of traffic; measure cost-per-1M-tokens, p50/p95/p99 latency, and tail-quality regressions via eval prompts.
- Key metrics: unit compute cost, batch fill rate, average effective padding ratio (wasted tokens / total), cache hit ratio, request queuing time.

Rollout plan (incremental & safe):
1) Implement profiler + kernel metadata store and offline bench harness.
2) Implement server-side per-bucket enqueue and pad-to-bucket padding logic (no kernel switching yet) behind feature flag.
3) Beta: enable per-bucket kernel selection for one model on a small fleet. Monitor memory/regressions.
4) Gradually expand to more models/hardware and enable adaptive bucket recompute.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- How many buckets is optimal in practice? (6-8 starting point but needs experiments).
- Do we support ragged/no-pad kernels in the short term or rely on pad-to-bucket? Ragged kernels are attractive but higher implementation complexity.
- Precise kv cache key semantics for minimal invalidations while preserving correctness.
- Alignment tradeoffs: when to force pow2 alignment for kernels that prefer it?

Implementation TODOs (short):
- [ ] Build offline kernel profiler harness and run for top-10 deployed models (Ben).
- [ ] Add per-model bucket config schema and storage (Anita).
- [ ] Implement per-bucket request queues and small coalescing windows (Sofia/Marcus).
- [ ] Define KV cache key/version semantics and migration plan (Luis).
- [ ] Add end-to-end A/B experiment and monitoring dashboards (obs team).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft; expect gaps in KV migration details and perf knobs. Prefer feedback on the bucketing + kernel mapping approach and scheduler integration.
- If we choose to support ragged inputs, call out additional kernel interfaces that the runtime needs (per-request offsets, compact KV layout).
